# On Forgetting

In 1942, Jorge Luis Borges published a short story about a young man in Uruguay named Ireneo Funes, who was thrown from a horse one afternoon and woke up with a broken body and a perfect memory. Not a good memory. A perfect one. Funes remembered everything that ever happened to him, and everything he ever perceived, forever. He could reconstruct every cloud he had watched cross the sky. He remembered not only every leaf of every tree, but every individual occasion on which he had looked at each leaf. His memory, Borges writes, was like a garbage heap.

And it ruined him. Funes, the story tells us, was "almost incapable of ideas of a general, Platonic sort." He could not grasp that the dog seen from the side at three o'clock in the afternoon and the dog seen from the front at four was the same dog. They were two separate facts, each complete, each self-contained, requiring their own names. He invented a number system in which numbers were not counted but christened: instead of saying seven thousand thirteen, he would say *Máximo Pérez*; instead of seven thousand fourteen, *The Train*. He understood that the project was doomed, since every number would need its own arbitrary label, forever. He learned Latin, English, and French more or less on his own, from a dictionary and a grammar, and read Pliny for pleasure. He died young—twenty-one, Borges tells us—of congestion of the lungs.

The story is only a few pages long, and it contains, in a single sentence, an idea that has shadowed every conversation about memory since: *to think is to forget differences, to generalize, to abstract.* Funes forgets nothing, and therefore thinks almost nothing. He notices everything and connects nothing.

What I love about this is the reversal it performs on our ordinary assumptions. We talk about memory as an asset and forgetting as its failure—a leak, a flaw, the machinery breaking down. Borges's story argues the opposite: forgetting is the machinery. A memory that retains everything is not a superior memory; it is not a memory at all, really. It is an archive, and archives don't think. They only hold.

Nietzsche had already made a version of this argument. In his 1874 essay on the uses and disadvantages of history, he asks us to imagine the extreme case: a man who has entirely lost the power of forgetting, who sees everything dissolving into a flux of points, who cannot draw a horizon around the present. Such a man, Nietzsche says, would be like a pupil of Heraclitus who hardly dares lift a finger—paralyzed by sheer accumulation. Without forgetting, he insisted, it is quite impossible to live at all. Happiness requires a horizon, and a horizon requires that most of what lies behind it sink into darkness. Cheerfulness, action, trust in the future: all of it depends on the past being *mostly gone*.

The strange thing is that real life eventually caught up with the fiction. In the 1920s, a Moscow newspaper editor noticed that one of his reporters never took notes. Not because he was lazy—the man simply remembered every instruction, every fact, every name, without apparent effort. The editor sent him to the psychologist Alexander Luria, who spent the next thirty years trying and failing to find the limits of his memory. The reporter, Solomon Shereshevsky, could reproduce long strings of nonsense syllables years after hearing them once. But his gift was also, unmistakably, an affliction. He could barely recognize faces, because a face is a moving target—every change of expression made it a new face. He couldn't extract the gist of anything; he remembered exact wordings rather than meanings. Every word he heard summoned images so vivid they crowded out thought
